name: Thymogen

card.summary: A Glu-Trp dipeptide immunomodulator derived from the calf-thymus extract Thymalin; Russian drug lineage, animal and cell data, thin human evidence.
card.note: Described in the literature as a pharmaceutical; not approved in the US or EU as far as sources show, and evidence is largely from one research network.

quick.overview:
Thymogen is the brand name of a synthetic dipeptide, glutamyl-tryptophan, isolated from the calf thymus preparation Thymalin and then made synthetically. It is described as an immune system modulator.

Research is mostly animal and cell work from Khavinson's group; one rat study reported slower ageing and fewer spontaneous tumours. It has no documented appearance use.
quick.mechanism: Reported to activate T-cell differentiation, alter intracellular cyclic nucleotides and activate neutrophil chemotaxis [1]. It has also been grouped among interferon-inducing immunomodulators developed in former socialist countries [2].
quick.risks: No systematic safety data in the sources; it is not approved in the US or EU.

lead: Thymogen is the brand name of a pharmaceutical based on the synthetic dipeptide L-glutamyl-L-tryptophan (Glu-Trp), which Vladimir Khavinson's group isolated from the calf-thymus extract Thymalin and then synthesised.[1][3] It is characterised as an immunostimulant and sits within the family of short peptide 'bioregulators' developed at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology.[4][8]

In longevity and anti-ageing circles, Thymogen is of interest because the thymus shrinks with age and thymic peptides are proposed to restore immune function, and because one rat study associated the dipeptide with slower ageing and fewer spontaneous tumours.[3] The chain proponents of peptide bioregulators describe runs from supporting thymus and immune function, to slower biological ageing, to a healthier and younger-looking appearance; the published work cited here addresses immune and ageing endpoints rather than skin or hair.[3][8]

Most published material is Russian-language clinical work in infection and inflammation, plus animal and cell studies from the same research network.[16][17][18][3][5] A review places Thymogen among interferon-inducing immunomodulators developed mainly in former socialist countries and little known in the West.[2]

paras: Thymogen contains the dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp, obtained originally from Thymalin by reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography and then synthesised.[3] A 2024 review discusses it with Thymodepressin (D-Glu-D-Trp) as an example of enantiomeric peptide drugs that act in opposite directions: Thymogen as an immunostimulant and Thymodepressin as an immunosuppressor.[4]

The dipeptide was reported to activate T-cell differentiation and T-cell recognition of peptide-MHC complexes, change intracellular cyclic nucleotide levels and stimulate neutrophil chemotaxis.[3] Reviews group it with immunomodulators that act through interferon induction.[2] A 2010 review compares pineal peptides (epithalamin, epitalon) with thymic peptides (thymalin, thymogen) on involution of the thymus and pineal gland, concluding that pineal peptides had the more effective geroprotective effect on the thymus than thymic peptides had on the pineal gland.[13]

A 1997 review describes how Thymalin, a calf-thymus peptide complex, was used as an immunocorrector; the dipeptide L-Glu-L-Trp was isolated from it by chromatography, and Thymogen was designed on the basis of the synthesised dipeptide.[1] A second synthetic dipeptide, Vilon, followed.[1]

Wikipedia's article on Khavinson (1946 to 2024) describes him as director of the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, whose team between roughly 1973 and 2013 extracted peptide complexes from animal organs and synthesised others. It says these preparations were first used on military personnel exposed to radiation or toxic substances and that six peptide medicines were approved in the USSR and Russia; it also notes that claims of no toxic or adverse effects rest on the group's own studies.[12]

In rats the dipeptide was reported to slow ageing and inhibit spontaneous tumour development.[3] A 1992 Russian study examined the effect of Thymogen on radiation-induced carcinogenesis in rats.[14] A 2022 study in the THP-1 human monocyte/macrophage line compared Thymogen with Epitalon, Vilon, Thymalin and Chonluten for effects on proliferation and inflammatory pathways.[5] A 2023 report examined new analogues of Thymogen in an experimental model of liver damage.[15] Other Russian-language reports include effects of thymus preparations on experimental tuberculosis [6] and on stress behaviour in mice when combined with other agents.[7]

Clinical reports on Thymogen are small, Russian-language studies indexed in PubMed. In 46 patients with acute endomyometritis, exacerbations of chronic salpingo-oophoritis and purulent tubo-ovarian formations, Thymogen added to combined therapy was reported to normalise lymphocyte counts, increase T-lymphocyte functional activity, show a desensitising effect and cause no complications.[16]

A 1999 study in destructive pulmonary tuberculosis reported that Thymogen stimulated the T-cell link, improved tolerance of anti-tuberculosis drugs, resolved intoxication syndromes and helped heal cavities.[17] Other reports cover chronic suppurative obstructive bronchitis, soft-tissue purulent wounds, and pre-operative preparation of elderly patients with abdominal tumours (listed as a randomized controlled trial).[18][19][20]

A review summarises the authors' long-term clinical studies of peptide bioregulators (Thymalin, Thymogen, Vilon, Epithalamin and others) as a class, with attention to geroprotective use.[8] No trial testing Thymogen for appearance, skin or hair outcomes was found.

Thymogen is discussed as one of a set of Khavinson-lineage peptides alongside Epitalon, Vilon and Thymalin, often under the heading of peptide bioregulators for longevity.[5][8] Reviews describe its lineage as largely a Russian research network, with little independent replication in Western journals.[2]

chain: Synthetic Glu-Trp dipeptide acts as an immune modulator
Supports T-cell function in an ageing immune system
Proposed slower ageing and overall vitality, claimed to show in appearance
angle.text: Users interested in peptide bioregulators view Thymogen as part of an anti-ageing approach centred on thymus and immune support. Any effect on looks is claimed and indirect, through ageing and general health; published studies address immune and survival endpoints.
